name: thread-safe-interface
intent: Keep a component's locking discipline out of its internal call graph: public interface methods acquire the component's lock once at the border and delegate to implementation methods that never re-acquire it, so intra-component calls cannot self-deadlock and never pay for a second acquisition.
problem: A multi-threaded component guards its state with one lock, and every method that touches that state takes the lock. When such a method calls another method of the same component, the lock is re-acquired: a non-recursive mutex deadlocks the component against itself, and a recursive mutex makes the nested calls legal but pays lock-count bookkeeping for every one of them while hiding the design problem.
context: Concurrent components that own mutable state, guard it with a single lock and contain intra-component method calls - caches, registries, buffers, pools. It matters most where the lock must stay non-recursive (default POSIX, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Python and Swift mutexes) or where lock traffic must stay minimal, and it applies whenever the synchronization mechanism is chosen independently of the component logic (Strategized Locking), including a Null Mutex for single-threaded deployments.
benefits: Removes the self-deadlock failure mode by construction: with a non-recursive lock, an intra-component call cannot re-acquire what the component already holds, because implementation methods never lock.
Avoids the recursive-mutex crutch and its costs: no lock-count bookkeeping, no portability dependency on recursive mutex support, and no hidden double acquisition.
One lock acquisition per component entry instead of one per internal call - the minimal-locking-overhead half of the pattern (POSA2).
The locking boundary becomes explicit and reviewable: every lock site is a public method, and the internal precondition is a single documented rule.
Keeps the component's invariants continuously true inside a public operation, because the lock is not released between internal steps.
Lock-strategy independent: because the component never relies on re-entrancy, the same structure works with a plain mutex, a readers/writer lock or a Null Mutex.
tradeoffs: Every interface method needs at least one implementation method, so the component grows a second method family and each call gains a level of indirection (POSA2's single stated liability).

The 'lock is held' precondition is unchecked in almost every language: calling an implementation method directly from a subclass, friend, test or callback is a silent data race that no compiler, runtime or linter reports.

Re-entrancy through callbacks is not solved by the split: invoking a listener, virtual method or foreign call while holding the lock can bring control back into a public method and deadlock (or, with a reentrant lock, silently inflate the hold count).

The split constrains inheritance: an implementation method that calls a virtual or public method breaks the discipline, so template-method-style extension points have to be designed around the family boundary.

The discipline erodes under maintenance: a newly added public method that locks and then calls another public method, or an implementation method that re-adds a guard, reintroduces exactly the bug the pattern removed.
Where public methods do not call each other, the split buys nothing over one lock acquisition per public method.

participants.responsibility: Owns the guarded state and the lock; publishes the interface methods and keeps the implementation family internal.
Public entry point: acquires the component's lock at the border (scope-bound), forwards to its implementation method and releases the lock on every exit path.
Performs the actual work assuming the lock is held; never acquires or releases the lock and never calls an interface method.

The synchronization mechanism (mutex, recursive mutex, readers/writer lock, semaphore, null mutex) serialising access to the component's state; typically strategized so the component does not depend on one lock type.
Calls interface methods only; never holds the component's lock and never touches implementation methods.

use_cases: Cache components where a public lookup inserts on a miss through internal bind/check helpers (the POSA2 file-cache example).
Bounded buffers and queues whose public put/get share bookkeeping helpers and condition signalling.
Registry and metrics objects whose update methods fan out into several internal mutations that must be atomic with the update.
Connection and object pools whose acquire operation validates and replaces dead entries through internal helpers.
In-memory indexes (inverted index, LRU, session table) where lookups trigger maintenance work.
Components instantiated with a pluggable lock strategy, including a Null Mutex for single-threaded deployments.

CPython's free-threaded runtime splits its internal object APIs into locking entry points and *_LockHeld helpers (_PyDict_SetItem_LockHeld, _PyDict_Clear_LockHeld) that the caller may invoke only while holding the per-object or global lock.

Linux kernel subsystems: public functions acquire the lock and call internal helpers whose documentation states the caller must already hold it, the calling convention described in the kernel-hacking locking guide.

Go components built on sync.Mutex: the package documents the mutex as non-reentrant - a goroutine holding it that calls Lock again blocks forever - so exported methods lock at the border and delegate to unexported helpers that assume the lock is held.
avoid_when: The language's locks are reentrant and repeated acquisition is not a cost you care about (Java, C#, Scala): a plain synchronized/lock method is simpler and the self-deadlock force does not exist.
The public methods do not call each other: one acquisition per method is already minimal and the split adds only a second method family.
The state can be confined to one thread or goroutine (Thread Confinement) or owned by one actor/goroutine, so no lock is needed at all.
The state can be made immutable or replaced by a lock-free or concurrent data structure (immutability, copy-on-write, lock-free queue, concurrent collections).
The component is a thin facade that delegates elsewhere; the object that really owns the state is the right place for the locking discipline.
anti_patterns: Public methods that lock and then call other public methods of the same component: the classic violation, deadlocking on a non-recursive mutex.

Switching to a recursive mutex (std::recursive_mutex, PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE, RLock, NSRecursiveLock, reentrant Monitor) so that self-calls work: it hides the double acquisition, adds lock-count bookkeeping, and POSIX warns that an implicit unlock during a condition-variable wait may not release a mutex locked more than once.

Exposing implementation methods in the public API or documenting them as 'call only while holding the lock': the precondition escapes the component and the discipline dies with the first external caller.
Invoking callbacks, listeners or virtual methods while holding the lock; re-entrancy then arrives from outside the component.
Keeping two method families but letting them drift - interface methods that no longer lock, implementation methods that re-lock - with no ownership assertion, lock-type check or lint to catch it.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: synchronization policy at the component border, computation inside.
POSA2's two conventions: interface methods check (acquire, release, forward), implementation methods trust (assume the lock is held, never lock, never call interface methods).
Information hiding: the 'lock is held' precondition is internal; only the component's own code needs to know it.
Invariant preservation: the lock is not released between steps of a compound operation, so intermediate states are never observable.
Do not rely on implicit runtime semantics (re-entrancy, recursive mutexes) for correctness.
best_practices: Name the implementation family consistently (find_impl, bind_i, findLocked) and state 'the caller must hold the lock' at each definition.
Acquire through a scope-bound guard (Scoped Locking) so exceptions and early returns always release.
Never call an interface method from an implementation method; extract the needed work into another implementation method instead.
Keep callbacks, listener notifications and foreign calls outside the locked region, or make them lock-free by design.

Where the language allows it, encode the precondition: pass the guard or borrow into the implementation method (Rust's MutexGuard, a std::lock_guard& parameter, a Swift inout table) so a violation fails loudly or fails to compile.
Choose detection aids deliberately: PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK in debug builds, ownership assertions, or an architecture test that implementation methods are only called from inside the component.
When the component's operations stop being atomic together, split the component instead of growing the lock scope.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture, Volume 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (Wiley, 2000) - Thread-Safe Interface (Synchronization Patterns chapter).
